lead: Most machine learning failures come from data and generalization, not from the algorithm alone. A model can fit its training rows and still fail on a new customer, a new city or next month's traffic. This chapter lists the common challenges: small or noisy data, missing values, imbalanced classes, overfitting and underfitting, the bias-variance trade-off, high dimensionality, feature scaling, data leakage, concept drift and poor evaluation. These checks matter in UPI fraud detection, IRCTC demand forecasts and a Chennai power-cut predictor. The goal is a model that works on unseen data.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for the design cycle and performance measure.

blocks.text: A model is useful only if it works on data it has not seen. Training error is error on the rows used for fitting; validation error is error on held-out rows. Underfitting means the model is too simple: both errors are high. Overfitting means the model is too flexible: training error is low but validation error is high. The gap validation error minus training error measures overfitting. Bias is error from wrong assumptions. Variance is error from sensitivity to the training sample. More complex models usually lower bias and raise variance. The bias-variance trade-off picks the complexity that minimises total error. See Unit 2 for the full derivation, regularization and cross-validation.

blocks.where: y is the true target; f̂(x) is the model prediction; bias is the average gap between the true rule and the model's average prediction; variance is how much the prediction changes across training samples; σ² is unavoidable noise.

blocks.text: The figure plots both errors against model complexity. At complexity 3, validation error is 0.12, close to training error 0.10. At complexity 5, training error is 0.04 but validation error is 0.25. At complexity 9, training error falls to 0.01 but validation error rises to 0.45. That is overfitting: the model has learned detail that does not generalise.

Data problems cause most failures. With small data, a sample of 30 loan applications cannot support a rule with hundreds of features; variance dominates. Noisy labels teach wrong patterns: one mislabelled UPI fraud record is a wrong lesson. Missing values are common; a sensor can fail during a Chennai power cut. Dropping rows loses information, and mean filling can distort distributions. Imbalanced classes need care: if fraud is 1 in 1000 transactions, a model that always says 'not fraud' is 99.9% accurate and catches nothing. Use precision, recall or F1, and resample with care. The curse of dimensionality means that as features grow, data become sparse. Distance-based methods such as kNN lose meaning because nearest and farthest neighbours become similar. Feature scaling puts features on comparable ranges; a salary in rupees can dominate age in years. Standardise or normalise using training statistics only. See Unit 4 for dimensionality reduction and Unit 2 for metrics.

Evaluation must mimic deployment. Data leakage happens when information from the test set or the target leaks into training. A common slip is scaling features using all data before splitting, or using a future transaction to predict a past one. Keep the test set untouched and use it once. Concept drift means the relation between features and target changes over time. A model for electricity demand in Chennai learns summer patterns but fails after a new tariff or a heat wave. Monitor error and feature distributions, then retrain on recent data. Domain shift means test data come from a different source than training data, such as a model trained on Delhi traffic applied to Chennai. Only a few universities teach domain shift under this name. Evaluation choice matters: accuracy hides imbalance, and one split can be lucky. Use cross-validation and choose the metric that matches the cost of errors. Full treatment in Unit 2.

figure.caption: Training error keeps falling; validation error falls to a minimum near complexity 3 and then rises, which marks overfitting.

spec.aria: A plot of training error falling steadily and validation error first falling then rising as model complexity grows.

examples.question: A polynomial model is fitted at three degrees. Degree 1: training error 0.30, validation error 0.32. Degree 3: training error 0.10, validation error 0.12. Degree 9: training error 0.01, validation error 0.45. Compute the generalization gap for each degree. Which model underfits, which is a good fit, and which overfits?
steps: Gap = validation error − training error. Errors are unitless.
Degree 1 has gap 0.02, but both errors are high (0.30 and 0.32), so it underfits.
Degree 3 has low training and validation error, so it is a good fit.
Degree 9 has low training error 0.01 but high validation error 0.45 and gap 0.44, so it overfits.
examples.answer: The gaps are 0.02, 0.02 and 0.44 (unitless); degree 1 underfits, degree 3 is a good fit, and degree 9 overfits.

traps: Judging a model by training error alone. Low training error can mean overfitting, not a better model.
Calling every validation failure overfitting. If training and validation error are both high, the model underfits.
Scaling or filling missing values before the train-test split. That leaks test information into training.
Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data. A majority-class predictor can look strong and be useless.
Confusing concept drift with noise. Drift is a change in the feature-target relation, not random label errors.

quiz.a: Overfitting is when training error is low but validation error is high, so the model does not generalise.
Feature scaling puts features on comparable ranges, for example by standardisation or normalisation.

quiz.q: Why can accuracy mislead on an imbalanced fraud dataset?
quiz.a: If fraud is rare, predicting 'not fraud' for all cases gives high accuracy but zero fraud detection.

quiz.q: Training error is 0.10 and validation error is 0.12 for model A; training error is 0.01 and validation error is 0.45 for model B. Compute both gaps and say which overfits.
quiz.a: Model A gap = 0.12 − 0.10 = 0.02. Model B gap = 0.45 − 0.01 = 0.44. Model B overfits.

quiz.q: A model uses 500 features and only 40 training rows. Name two challenges and one remedy.
quiz.a: Challenges: the curse of dimensionality makes data sparse, and small data raises variance or overfitting. Remedy: reduce features, collect more data, or use regularization; see Unit 2 and Unit 4.

quiz.q: How does data leakage differ from concept drift?
quiz.a: Data leakage is information contamination between training and evaluation. Concept drift is a change over time in the relation between features and target.

quiz.q: A test set is used to tune 20 models, and the best test score is reported. What is wrong and what should be done?
quiz.a: The test set has leaked into model selection, so its score is optimistic. Tune on a validation set or with cross-validation, then use the test set once.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, most of the work is data quality: label audits, drift dashboards and feature stores. Search for 'data-centric AI', 'concept drift detection' and 'leakage in machine learning pipelines'. Research on robustness studies domain shift and distribution shift. Newer curricula add MLOps monitoring, because a deployed model meets changing data every day.
